title: Looking for help finding the proper way to describe something which I do not even know enough about to know how to Google search for it, but I can describe it. Related to cinematography/editing.

commenti.body:
I guess this editing decision has no particular name because it is very specific and circunstancial of this film and this scene. I can only offer an explanation on why it could be there. 

I’m assuming it definitely has a humorous intention. It is a visual gag precisely because it breaks with the camera angles of the rest of the shots and therefore is meant to stand out but his short duration implies a comedic effect. I think it is funny because the character decides this small nugget of information is important, I don’t remember the context of the dialogue but I guess he has a prejudice against protestants? And he is looking for the old lady’s approval on his prejudice.

Well I think I overexplained it, hah. But for me it is clearly a filmmaking choice to ridicule the character or to point out his flawed nature. The director could have kept that line of dialogue in the previous shot but deciding to cut to another one, and one that is so visually different, is like putting an accent on that particular line. Very nice little moment indeed.

Exactly. I think if I were to try and describe the effect that using that cut has on the meaning of the dialogue would be that, as you said it definitely implies that he is prejudice against Protestants, but to me it felt like it was winking at you as if the policeman also said to Mrs. McCormick (without actually saying it) "*you* know what I'm talking about, Mrs. McCormick. *You're* on our team."

I was kind of hoping that it had some catchy name, like, "oh, that's called a Monkey Cut" or something like that lol. Obviously I made that up but you get the point.

And also, yes I agree, it somehow takes this not-so-funny character and creates a funny, tiny little visual joke out of thin air. The downward angle combined with the smug aura that the policeman seems to always exude in every scene he's in just felt like the perfect match. I can't say for sure, but I *think* that may be the only camera angle looking *up* at the policeman in the whole film. Unless you count the part just a scene later when he's directly on top of Padraic, giving him that battering, but the *angle* of that shot doesn't feel as if you're looking up at him in the same way because it's from Padraic's POV. He's flat on his back (or at least flat on the ground in some way), so the policeman is directly in front of the camera, same as he'd be if he were standing in front of you. Not above it, as in the cut I asked about.

I believe the technical term would be an insert since it reverts back to the original shot right after he turns to say "Protestant, of course." It was definitely inserted for some kind of comedic effect or to push the action of his conversation.
Right on! A name! Makes sense, too. An insert. I'll definitely check that channel out, thanks :)

An insert is usually a shot of an object, like if a character is looking at their phone or a note, you would shoot an "insert" of said object. I've never heard the term being used in regards to a shot of an actor like the one attached.
Wouldn't that be a cut in or a cut away though?

From what you’ve described, it seems like this particular cut might be using a technique known as a **“motivated cut”**. This is where the cut is driven by a character’s action or gaze, creating a seamless and natural transition that feels “right” to the viewer. In this case, the policeman’s sudden turn and look towards Mrs. McCormick, followed by the cut to a lower angle, might be intended to draw the audience’s attention to her reaction and to emphasize the significance of his words.

Additionally, the use of a lower camera angle can create a sense of intimacy or vulnerability, making the audience feel as if they are in the scene with the characters. This technique can be particularly effective in drawing the viewer into the story and enhancing the emotional impact of the moment.

I would say a cutaway is more like a shot that is away from the main action. So an insert is the shot of the phone when the character is looking at it. A cutaway would be a shot of a phone if the character wasn't interacting with it, if it was in another part of the room, or lost somewhere.

I'm just basing this off what I've heard people say on sets and in editing over the years. "Okay, let's shoot an insert" I've only ever heard used in the context I've described.
Yeah. Someone else mentioned describing it as a motivation cut or motivation shot. That sounds more apt for this scenario.
The movie this makes me think of is The Matrix. Whenever they're inside it and a phone rings: cutaway on the phone ringing.
